docs.title: 💡 Core Principles for AP Physics Success
docs.text:
• Algebraic Derivations Before Numbers: AP Physics 1 Free-Response Questions predominantly test symbolic manipulation rather than arithmetic computation.
  • Graph Interpretation:
    • Position-Time (\(x\)-\(t\)): Slope is velocity (\(v = \frac{dx}{dt}\)).
    • Velocity-Time (\(v\)-\(t\)): Slope is acceleration (\(a = \frac{dv}{dt}\)); Area under curve is displacement (\(\Delta x = \int v\,dt\)).
    • Acceleration-Time (\(a\)-\(t\)): Area under curve is change in velocity (\(\Delta v = \int a\,dt\)).
    • Force-Position (\(F\)-\(x\)): Area under curve is work done (\(W = \int F\,dx\)).
    • Force-Time (\(F\)-\(t\)): Area under curve is impulse (\(\vec{J} = \Delta\vec{p}\)).
  • Sign Conventions: Establish a coordinate system at the beginning of every problem and adhere to it strictly.

docs.title: Unit 1: Kinematics
docs.text: Kinematics describes the motion of objects without reference to the forces causing that motion. We analyze position (\(x\)), velocity (\(v\)), acceleration (\(a\)), and time (\(t\)).

docs.title: 1.1 The Fundamental Kinematic Equations
docs.text:
For motion with constant acceleration (\(a = \text{const}\)), the AP Physics 1 equation sheet provides three core equations:

\[v_x = v_{0x} + a_x t\] \[x = x_0 + v_{0x} t + \frac{1}{2} a_x t^2\] \[v_x^2 = v_{0x}^2 + 2 a_x (x - x_0)\]

Additionally, when acceleration is constant, the average velocity equals the arithmetic mean:

\[\bar{v}_x = \frac{v_x + v_{0x}}{2} \implies \Delta x = \left(\frac{v_x + v_{0x}}{2}\right) t\]

docs.title: 1.2 Two-Dimensional Projectile Motion
docs.text:
In 2D projectile motion near Earth's surface (neglecting air resistance): - Horizontal Axis (\(x\)): Zero acceleration (\(a_x = 0\)), constant velocity. - Vertical Axis (\(y\)): Constant downward gravitational acceleration (\(a_y = -g = -9.8\,\text{m/s}^2\)).

\[\begin{aligned} v_{0x} &= v_0 \cos\theta, & x(t) &= (v_0 \cos\theta) t \\ v_{0y} &= v_0 \sin\theta, & y(t) &= y_0 + (v_0 \sin\theta) t - \frac{1}{2} g t^2 \end{aligned}\]

AP Exam Trap: Horizontal vs. Vertical Independence

Remember that the horizontal and vertical motions are completely independent except for the shared variable: time (\(t\)).

A common trap on multiple-choice questions asks: "If bullet A is fired horizontally and bullet B is dropped from the same height at the exact same instant, which hits the ground first?"

Both hit the ground at the exact same time because both start with \(v_{0y} = 0\) and experience identical vertical acceleration \(a_y = -g\).

docs.title: 📝 Practice Problem & Solution
docs.text:
Practice Problem 1.1: Cliff Projectile Motion

A rescue ball is launched from the edge of a cliff of height \(H = 45\,\text{m}\) with an initial velocity \(v_0 = 20\,\text{m/s}\) at an angle of \(\theta = 30^\circ\) above the horizontal. Assume \(g = 10\,\text{m/s}^2\) and negligible air resistance.

a. Calculate the total time of flight before the ball strikes the level ground below. b. Determine the horizontal distance (range) traveled by the ball.

Show Step-by-Step Solution

Step 1: Decompose the initial velocity vector:

\[\begin{aligned} v_{0x} &= v_0 \cos(30^\circ) = 20 \cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 10\sqrt{3}\,\text{m/s} \approx 17.32\,\text{m/s} \\ v_{0y} &= v_0 \sin(30^\circ) = 20 \cdot \frac{1}{2} = 10\,\text{m/s} \end{aligned}\]

Step 2: Solve for time of flight using vertical motion:

Set the origin at the ground below the cliff so \(y_0 = 45\,\text{m}\) and \(y(t) = 0\):

\[y(t) = y_0 + v_{0y} t - \frac{1}{2} g t^2\] \[0 = 45 + 10t - \frac{1}{2}(10) t^2 \implies -5t^2 + 10t + 45 = 0\]

Divide through by \(-5\):

\[t^2 - 2t - 9 = 0\]

Apply the quadratic formula:

\[t = \frac{-(-2) \pm \sqrt{(-2)^2 - 4(1)(-9)}}{2(1)} = \frac{2 \pm \sqrt{4 + 36}}{2} = \frac{2 \pm \sqrt{40}}{2} = 1 \pm \sqrt{10}\]

Since time must be positive (\(t > 0\)):

\[t = 1 + \sqrt{10} \approx 1 + 3.162 = \mathbf{4.16\,\text{s}}\]

Step 3: Calculate horizontal range:

Since horizontal acceleration \(a_x = 0\):

\[\Delta x = v_{0x} \cdot t = (10\sqrt{3})(1 + \sqrt{10}) \approx 17.32 \times 4.162 \approx \mathbf{72.1\,\text{m}}\]

docs.title: Unit 2: Force & Translational Dynamics
docs.text: Dynamics investigates the relationship between forces and changes in the translational motion of bodies, governed by Newton's three fundamental laws of motion.

docs.title: 2.1 Systems & Center of Mass
docs.text:
A system is a collection of objects treated as a single entity. The center of mass (\(\vec{r}_{\text{cm}}\)) represents the average position of the system's mass:

\[x_{\text{cm}} = \frac{\sum m_i x_i}{\sum m_i} = \frac{m_1 x_1 + m_2 x_2 + \dots + m_n x_n}{M_{\text{total}}}\]

If the net external force on a system is zero (\(\sum \vec{F}_{\text{ext}} = 0\)), the velocity of the center of mass remains constant (\(\vec{v}_{\text{cm}} = \text{const}\)), regardless of internal interactions.

docs.title: 2.2 Free-Body Diagrams (FBDs)
docs.text: Free-body diagrams represent all external forces acting directly on an isolated object: - Forces must originate at the center of the object (or point of application) pointing outward. - Never include components on a graded AP Exam FBD unless explicitly asked; draw only the fundamental forces (\(F_g, F_N, F_T, F_f, F_s\)). - Never draw "centripetal force" (\(\vec{F}_c\)) or "net force" (\(\vec{F}_{\text{net}}\)) as physical forces.

docs.title: 2.3 Newton's Laws of Motion
docs.text:
1. Newton's First Law (Inertia): An object continues in a state of rest or uniform velocity unless acted upon by a non-zero net external force: $\(\sum \vec{F} = 0 \iff \vec{a} = 0 \quad (\text{Translational Equilibrium})\)$
  2. Newton's Second Law: The acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the net force and inversely proportional to its inertial mass: $\(\sum \vec{F} = m \vec{a} \implies \begin{cases} \sum F_x = m a_x \\ \sum F_y = m a_y \end{cases}\)$
  3. Newton's Third Law: When body \(A\) exerts force \(\vec{F}_{A \to B}\) on body \(B\), body \(B\) exerts an equal and opposite force on body \(A\): $\(\vec{F}_{A \to B} = -\vec{F}_{B \to A}\)$ (Third-law action-reaction pairs act on different objects and never cancel each other on a single FBD).

docs.title: Contact Friction
docs.text: Friction opposes the relative sliding (or intended sliding) between two contact surfaces: - Static Friction (\(f_s\)): Self-adjusting force preventing sliding up to a maximum threshold: $\(f_s \le \mu_s F_N \implies f_{s,\text{max}} = \mu_s F_N\)$ - Kinetic Friction (\(f_k\)): Acts once surfaces slide across each other: $\(f_k = \mu_k F_N \quad (\text{with } \mu_k < \mu_s)\)$

docs.title: Hooke's Law (Ideal Springs)
docs.text:
An ideal spring produces a linear restoring force proportional to displacement from equilibrium:

\[\vec{F}_s = -k \Delta\vec{x}\]

where \(k\) is the spring constant (\(\text{N/m}\)) and \(\Delta x\) is the extension or compression.

docs.title: 2.5 Uniform Circular Motion & Gravitation
docs.text:
An object moving in a circle of radius \(r\) at constant speed \(v\) undergoes continuous centripetal acceleration directed toward the center of curvature:

\[a_c = \frac{v^2}{r} = \omega^2 r\]

The required net inward radial force is provided by real physical forces (e.g., tension, gravity, normal force, friction):

\[\sum F_{\text{radial}} = m a_c = \frac{m v^2}{r}\]

docs.title: Newton's Universal Law of Gravitation
docs.text:
Every pair of point masses attracts with a mutual gravitational force inversely proportional to the square of their center-to-center separation \(r\):

\[F_g = G \frac{m_1 m_2}{r^2} \quad \left(G \approx 6.674 \times 10^{-11}\,\text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{kg}^2\right)\]

At the surface of a spherical planet of mass \(M\) and radius \(R\):

\[g = G \frac{M}{R^2}\]

AP Exam Trap: Normal Force is Not Automatically Equal to \(mg\)

Students frequently assume \(F_N = mg\). The normal force is a constraint force whose magnitude adjusts based on all vertical forces:

  • On a horizontal surface with a downward push at angle \(\theta\): \(F_N = mg + F\sin\theta\).
  • On a ramp inclined at angle \(\theta\): \(F_N = mg \cos\theta\).
  • Inside an elevator accelerating upward at \(a\): \(F_N = m(g + a)\).

Always set up \(\sum F_y = m a_y\) from your FBD to solve for \(F_N\) algebraically before computing friction!

docs.title: 📝 Practice Problem & Solution
docs.text:
Practice Problem 2.1: Block on an Incline with Friction

A crate of mass \(m = 10\,\text{kg}\) is placed on an incline tilted at an angle of \(\theta = 37^\circ\) above the horizontal (\(\sin 37^\circ \approx 0.60\), \(\cos 37^\circ \approx 0.80\)). The coefficients of friction between the crate and the incline are \(\mu_s = 0.50\) and \(\mu_k = 0.30\). Take \(g = 10\,\text{m/s}^2\).

a. Determine whether the crate remains at rest or begins to slide down the ramp. b. If the crate slides, calculate the magnitude of its acceleration down the incline.

Show Step-by-Step Solution

Part a: Check if the block slides (Static vs. Driving Force):

Set up a tilted coordinate system with the \(x\)-axis pointing down the ramp and the \(y\)-axis perpendicular to the ramp:

  1. Perpendicular forces (\(y\)-axis): $\(\sum F_y = F_N - mg\cos\theta = 0 \implies F_N = mg\cos\theta\)$ $\(F_N = (10)(10)(\cos 37^\circ) = (100)(0.80) = 80\,\text{N}\)$

  2. Maximum static friction: $\(f_{s,\text{max}} = \mu_s F_N = (0.50)(80\,\text{N}) = 40\,\text{N}\)$

  3. Gravitational component down the incline (\(x\)-axis): $\(F_{g,\parallel} = mg\sin\theta = (10)(10)(\sin 37^\circ) = (100)(0.60) = 60\,\text{N}\)$

Since \(F_{g,\parallel} = 60\,\text{N} > f_{s,\text{max}} = 40\,\text{N}\), static friction is overcome and the crate slides down the incline.

Part b: Calculate acceleration down the incline:

Once the crate slides, kinetic friction opposes the motion:

\[f_k = \mu_k F_N = (0.30)(80\,\text{N}) = 24\,\text{N}\]

Apply Newton's Second Law along the parallel axis:

\[\sum F_x = mg\sin\theta - f_k = m a_x\] \[60\,\text{N} - 24\,\text{N} = (10\,\text{kg}) a_x\] \[36 = 10 a_x \implies a_x = \mathbf{3.6\,\text{m/s}^2}\]

docs.title: Unit 3: Work, Energy, & Power
docs.text: Energy is a scalar quantity that characterizes the ability of a system to undergo transformations. Work represents the mechanical mechanism of transferring energy into or out of a defined system.

docs.title: 3.1 Work Done by a Force
docs.text:
The mechanical work (\(W\)) done by a constant force \(\vec{F}\) acting on an object displaced by \(\Delta\vec{r}\) is defined by the vector dot product:

\[W = \vec{F} \cdot \Delta\vec{r} = F \|\Delta\vec{r}\| \cos\theta\]

where \(\theta\) is the angle between the force vector and the displacement vector: - Positive Work (\(\theta < 90^\circ\)): Force adds kinetic energy to the object. - Zero Work (\(\theta = 90^\circ\)): Perpendicular forces (such as the normal force on a flat horizontal track or centripetal tension in circular motion) do no work. - Negative Work (\(\theta > 90^\circ\)): Opposing forces (such as kinetic friction) remove kinetic energy from the object.

docs.title: Work from a Variable Force Graph
docs.text:
For a position-dependent force \(F(x)\), the work equals the area under the Force vs. Position curve:

\[W = \int_{x_i}^{x_f} F(x)\,dx\]

docs.title: 3.2 Kinetic Energy & The Work-Energy Theorem
docs.text:
The translational kinetic energy (\(K\)) of an object of mass \(m\) moving at speed \(v\) is:

\[K = \frac{1}{2} m v^2\]

docs.title: The Work-Energy Theorem
docs.text:
The net external work done on a single point-like object equals the net change in its kinetic energy:

\[W_{\text{net}} = \sum W_i = \Delta K = K_f - K_i = \frac{1}{2}m v_f^2 - \frac{1}{2}m v_i^2\]

docs.title: 3.3 Conservative Forces & Potential Energies
docs.text:
A force is conservative if the work it does on an object moving between two points is path-independent (or zero around any closed loop):

\[W_{\text{conservative}} = -\Delta U = -(U_f - U_i)\]
  1. Gravitational Potential Energy (\(U_g\)): For an object of mass \(m\) near Earth's surface relative to reference height \(y = 0\): $\(U_g = m g h\)$
  2. Elastic Potential Energy (\(U_s\)): For an ideal spring of stiffness \(k\) compressed or stretched by displacement \(x\): $\(U_s = \frac{1}{2} k x^2\)$

docs.title: 3.4 Conservation of Mechanical Energy
docs.text:
The total mechanical energy of a system is the sum of its kinetic and potential energies:

\[E_{\text{mech}} = K + U = K + U_g + U_s\]

docs.title: System Boundary Choices
docs.text:
• Closed (Isolated) System: When no external non-conservative forces do work on the system (\(W_{\text{ext}} = 0\)): $\(E_i = E_f \iff K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f\)$
  • Open System with Non-Conservative Work: When friction or applied external forces act: $\(E_i + W_{\text{ext}} = E_f \implies K_i + U_i - f_k d = K_f + U_f\)$

docs.title: 3.5 Mechanical Power
docs.text:
Power (\(P\)) is the instantaneous or average rate at which work is performed or energy is transformed:

\[\bar{P} = \frac{\Delta E}{\Delta t} = \frac{W}{\Delta t}\]

For a constant driving force \(\vec{F}\) moving an object at velocity \(\vec{v}\):

\[P = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{v} = F v \cos\theta\]

AP Exam Tip: System Definition Dictates Whether Gravity is Work or Potential Energy

On Free-Response Question energy derivations, your choice of system defines the mathematical formulation:

  • System = Block: Earth is external to the system. Gravity is an external force that performs external work on the block: \(W_g = \Delta K\). There is no potential energy term!
  • System = Block + Earth: Gravity is an internal conservative force. The gravitational interaction is stored as potential energy: \(\Delta K + \Delta U_g = 0\).

Both choices yield identical final speeds, but mixing them (e.g., claiming both \(W_g\) and \(\Delta U_g\) are present) double-counts gravity and loses credit.

docs.title: 📝 Practice Problem & Solution
docs.text:
Practice Problem 3.1: Spring-Launched Cart with Friction

A cart of mass \(m = 2.0\,\text{kg}\) is pushed against a horizontal spring of spring constant \(k = 800\,\text{N/m}\), compressing it by \(x = 0.20\,\text{m}\).

Upon release from rest, the cart travels across a frictionless horizontal table, and then encounters a rough section of track of length \(d = 1.5\,\text{m}\) where the coefficient of kinetic friction is \(\mu_k = 0.25\). Finally, it glides smoothly up a frictionless curved ramp. Take \(g = 10\,\text{m/s}^2\).

a. Calculate the speed of the cart immediately after leaving the spring (before the rough section). b. Calculate the work done by friction as the cart traverses the rough section. c. Determine the maximum vertical height \(h_{\text{max}}\) the cart reaches on the frictionless ramp.

Show Step-by-Step Solution

Part a: Speed leaving the spring:

Define the system as the cart + spring + table (frictionless initially). Mechanical energy is conserved:

\[U_{s,i} = K_1 \implies \frac{1}{2} k x^2 = \frac{1}{2} m v_1^2\] \[v_1 = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}} x = \sqrt{\frac{800}{2.0}} (0.20) = \sqrt{400} (0.20) = (20)(0.20) = \mathbf{4.0\,\text{m/s}}\]

Part b: Work done by kinetic friction:

On the flat rough section, the normal force is \(F_N = mg = (2.0)(10) = 20\,\text{N}\).

The magnitude of the kinetic friction force is:

\[f_k = \mu_k F_N = (0.25)(20\,\text{N}) = 5.0\,\text{N}\]

Friction acts directly opposite to the displacement (\(\theta = 180^\circ\)):

\[W_f = -f_k \cdot d = -(5.0\,\text{N})(1.5\,\text{m}) = \mathbf{-7.5\,\text{J}}\]

Part c: Maximum vertical height on the ramp:

Apply the conservation of energy between the initial spring compression and the maximum height on the ramp (\(v_{\text{top}} = 0\)):

\[E_i + W_f = E_f\] \[U_{s,i} + W_f = U_{g,f}\] \[\frac{1}{2} k x^2 - 7.5\,\text{J} = m g h_{\text{max}}\]

Initial spring energy:

\[U_{s,i} = \frac{1}{2}(800)(0.20)^2 = 400(0.04) = 16.0\,\text{J}\]

Remaining mechanical energy entering the ramp:

\[E_{\text{ramp}} = 16.0\,\text{J} - 7.5\,\text{J} = 8.5\,\text{J}\]

Solve for \(h_{\text{max}}\):

\[8.5\,\text{J} = m g h_{\text{max}} = (2.0)(10) h_{\text{max}} = 20 h_{\text{max}}\] \[h_{\text{max}} = \frac{8.5}{20} = \mathbf{0.425\,\text{m}} = 42.5\,\text{cm}\]

docs.title: Unit 4: Linear Momentum
docs.text: Momentum is a fundamental vector quantity that measures an object's resistance to stopping, representing inertia in motion.

docs.title: 4.1 Linear Momentum & Impulse
docs.text:
The linear momentum (\(\vec{p}\)) of an object of mass \(m\) traveling with velocity \(\vec{v}\) is:

\[\vec{p} = m \vec{v}\]

Momentum is a vector quantity having the same direction as the velocity vector, measured in \(\text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}\) or \(\text{N}\cdot\text{s}\).

docs.title: The Impulse-Momentum Theorem
docs.text:
Newton's Second Law can be expressed in terms of momentum:

\[\vec{F}_{\text{net}} = \frac{\Delta\vec{p}}{\Delta t} \implies \vec{J} = \vec{F}_{\text{net}} \Delta t = \Delta\vec{p} = m\vec{v}_f - m\vec{v}_i\]

The vector Impulse (\(\vec{J}\)) produces a change in the momentum of the object: - For a variable force \(\vec{F}(t)\), the impulse equals the area under the Force vs. Time graph: $\(\vec{J} = \int_{t_i}^{t_f} \vec{F}(t)\,dt = \vec{F}_{\text{avg}} \Delta t\)$

docs.title: 4.2 Conservation of Linear Momentum
docs.text:
For a system of interacting particles, the internal forces between bodies occur in equal and opposite pairs by Newton's Third Law (\(\vec{F}_{12} = -\vec{F}_{21}\)).

If the net external force acting on the system is zero (\(\sum \vec{F}_{\text{ext}} = 0\)), the total linear momentum of the system is strictly conserved:

\[\sum \vec{p}_i = \sum \vec{p}_f \implies m_1 \vec{v}_{1i} + m_2 \vec{v}_{2i} = m_1 \vec{v}_{1f} + m_2 \vec{v}_{2f}\]

In two dimensions, momentum conservation holds independently along each orthogonal axis:

\[\sum p_{ix} = \sum p_{fx} \quad \text{and} \quad \sum p_{iy} = \sum p_{fy}\]

docs.title: 4.3 Center of Mass Velocity
docs.text:
The velocity of the center of mass of a system of particles is:

\[\vec{v}_{\text{cm}} = \frac{\sum m_i \vec{v}_i}{\sum m_i} = \frac{\vec{p}_{\text{total}}}{M_{\text{total}}}\]

In an isolated system (\(\vec{F}_{\text{ext}} = 0\)), the center of mass velocity cannot change:

\[\vec{v}_{\text{cm}} = \text{constant}\]

docs.title: 4.4 Classification of Collisions
docs.text:
Total momentum is conserved in all collisions within an isolated system. Collisions are classified by what happens to total mechanical kinetic energy:

Collision Type Momentum Conserved? Kinetic Energy Conserved? Key Physical Characteristics Elastic Yes Yes (\(K_i = K_f\)) Ideal atomic collisions, bouncy magnetic gliders Inelastic Yes No (\(K_f < K_i\)) Energy transformed into thermal, sound, deformation Completely Inelastic Yes Maximum \(K\) loss Bodies stick together and move with identical final velocity \(v_f\) Explosion / Separation Yes \(K_f > K_i\) Chemical/stored elastic potential energy converts to kinetic

docs.title: Completely Inelastic Collision Formula
docs.text:
When two masses collide and stick together:

\[m_1 v_{1i} + m_2 v_{2i} = (m_1 + m_2) v_f \implies v_f = \frac{m_1 v_{1i} + m_2 v_{2i}}{m_1 + m_2}\]

AP Exam Trap: Momentum is a Vector (Watch the Negative Signs!)

A frequent error on AP Physics 1 exams is treating momentum as a scalar when an object bounces off a barrier.

Consider a rubber ball of mass \(m\) striking a rigid wall with speed \(v\) and bouncing back with the same speed \(v\): - Initial momentum: \(p_i = +mv\) - Final momentum: \(p_f = -mv\) - Change in momentum (Impulse): $\(\Delta p = p_f - p_i = -mv - (+mv) = -2mv \quad (\text{Magnitude } 2mv)\)$

If you forget the negative direction of \(\vec{v}_f\), you will incorrectly calculate \(\Delta p = 0\)!

docs.title: 📝 Practice Problem & Solution
docs.text:
Practice Problem 4.1: The Ballistic Pendulum

In a classic laboratory ballistic pendulum experiment, a wooden block of mass \(M = 1.95\,\text{kg}\) is suspended from lightweight cords of length \(L = 1.2\,\text{m}\). A bullet of mass \(m = 0.05\,\text{kg}\) is fired horizontally with speed \(v_0\) into the block, embedding itself completely.

After the collision, the block + embedded bullet pendulum swings upward, reaching a maximum vertical height of \(h = 0.20\,\text{m}\). Take \(g = 10\,\text{m/s}^2\).

a. Determine the speed \(V\) of the block + bullet system immediately after the collision. b. Calculate the initial speed \(v_0\) of the bullet. c. Determine the amount of mechanical energy dissipated during the collision.

Show Step-by-Step Solution

Part a: Speed \(V\) immediately after collision (Energy Conservation during swing):

After the bullet embeds, external forces are gravity and tension (which does zero work because it is perpendicular to motion). Mechanical energy is conserved during the upward swing:

\[K_{\text{post-collision}} = U_{g,\text{top}}\] \[\frac{1}{2}(m + M) V^2 = (m + M) g h\] \[V = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{2(10)(0.20)} = \sqrt{4.0} = \mathbf{2.0\,\text{m/s}}\]

Part b: Initial speed \(v_0\) of the bullet (Momentum Conservation during collision):

During the collision impact, the collision time is infinitesimal (\(\Delta t \to 0\)), so external forces (gravity) impart negligible impulse. Total linear momentum is conserved:

\[p_{\text{initial}} = p_{\text{final}}\] \[m v_0 + M(0) = (m + M) V\] \[v_0 = \frac{m + M}{m} V = \frac{0.05 + 1.95}{0.05} (2.0) = \frac{2.00}{0.05} (2.0) = (40)(2.0) = \mathbf{80\,\text{m/s}}\]

Part c: Energy dissipated during collision:

  • Initial kinetic energy: $\(K_i = \frac{1}{2} m v_0^2 = \frac{1}{2}(0.05\,\text{kg})(80\,\text{m/s})^2 = \frac{1}{2}(0.05)(6{,}400) = 160\,\text{J}\)$

  • Kinetic energy immediately after collision: $\(K_f = \frac{1}{2}(m + M) V^2 = \frac{1}{2}(2.00\,\text{kg})(2.0\,\text{m/s})^2 = \frac{1}{2}(2.00)(4.0) = 4.0\,\text{J}\)$

  • Energy dissipated: $\(\Delta E_{\text{lost}} = K_i - K_f = 160\,\text{J} - 4.0\,\text{J} = \mathbf{156\,\text{J}}\)$

(Over \(97.5\%\) of the mechanical energy was dissipated into heat, deformation, and sound during the inelastic embedding).

docs.title: Unit 5: Torque & Rotational Dynamics
docs.text: Rotational dynamics extends translational mechanics to extended rigid bodies that rotate about a fixed axis or center of mass.

docs.title: 5.1 Rotational Kinematics
docs.text:
When an extended object rotates about a fixed axis, all points on the body undergo identical angular displacement (\(\theta\)), angular velocity (\(\omega\)), and angular acceleration (\(\alpha\)).

Angular Variable Translational Analogy (at radius \(r\)) Relationship Angular Position \(\theta\) (rad) Linear Arc Length \(s\) (m) \(s = r \theta\) Angular Velocity \(\omega\) (rad/s) Tangential Speed \(v_t\) (m/s) \(v_t = r \omega\) Angular Acceleration \(\alpha\) (\(\text{rad/s}^2\)) Tangential Acceleration \(a_t\) (\(\text{m/s}^2\)) \(a_t = r \alpha\) Centripetal Acceleration \(a_c\) Centripetal Acceleration \(a_c = \frac{v_t^2}{r} = \omega^2 r\)

docs.title: Constant Angular Acceleration Equations
docs.text:
For constant \(\alpha\):

\[\omega = \omega_0 + \alpha t\] \[\theta = \theta_0 + \omega_0 t + \frac{1}{2} \alpha t^2\] \[\omega^2 = \omega_0^2 + 2\alpha(\theta - \theta_0)\]

docs.title: 5.2 Torque
docs.text:
Torque (\(\vec{\tau}\)) is the quantitative measure of a force's effectiveness at causing or altering rotational motion about a designated pivot point:

\[\tau = r F \sin\theta = r_\perp F = r F_\perp\]

where: - \(r\) is the distance from the pivot point (axis of rotation) to the point where the force is applied. - \(\theta\) is the angle between the position vector \(\vec{r}\) and the force vector \(\vec{F}\). - \(r_\perp = r\sin\theta\) is the lever arm (perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force). - Sign Convention: Counterclockwise torques are standardly positive (\(+\)); clockwise torques are negative (\(-\)).

docs.title: 5.3 Rotational Inertia (Moment of Inertia)
docs.text:
Rotational inertia (\(I\)) measures an object's resistance to changes in its rotational state. It depends not only on total mass, but on how that mass is distributed relative to the axis of rotation:

\[I = \sum m_i r_i^2 = \int r^2\,dm\]

docs.title: Common Moments of Inertia (Mass \(M\), Radius \(R\))
docs.text:
• Hoop / Thin Cylindrical Shell (about central axis): \(I = M R^2\)
  • Solid Uniform Cylinder / Disk (about central axis): \(I = \frac{1}{2} M R^2\)
  • Solid Uniform Sphere (about diameter): \(I = \frac{2}{5} M R^2\)
  • Thin Hollow Spherical Shell: \(I = \frac{2}{3} M R^2\)
  • Thin Uniform Rod of length \(L\) (about center): \(I = \frac{1}{12} M L^2\)
  • Thin Uniform Rod of length \(L\) (about one end): \(I = \frac{1}{3} M L^2\)

docs.title: 5.4 Static Equilibrium
docs.text:
For an extended body to remain in complete static equilibrium (neither translating nor rotating):

\[\sum \vec{F}_x = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \sum \vec{F}_y = 0 \quad (\text{Translational Equilibrium})\] \[\sum \tau_{\text{pivot}} = 0 \quad (\text{Rotational Equilibrium})\]

(If an object is in translational equilibrium, the net torque is identical about any arbitrary pivot point).

docs.title: 5.5 Newton's Second Law for Rotation
docs.text:
When a non-zero net external torque acts on a rigid body of rotational inertia \(I\):

\[\sum \tau_{\text{net}} = I \alpha\]

AP Exam Tip: Choosing the Pivot to Eliminate Unknown Forces

When solving static equilibrium problems (such as a ladder resting against a wall or a sign hanging from a hinged strut):

Always place your reference pivot point at the location of an unknown, unrequested force (e.g., the hinge pin or the rough floor).

Because the distance \(r = 0\) for forces acting directly at the pivot, their torques are identically zero (\(\tau = 0\)). This removes those unknown forces from your torque balance equation, allowing you to solve for the target variable in a single equation!

docs.title: 📝 Practice Problem & Solution
docs.text:
Practice Problem 5.1: Massive Pulley with Hanging Mass

A uniform solid disk pulley of mass \(M = 4.0\,\text{kg}\) and radius \(R = 0.20\,\text{m}\) (\(I = \frac{1}{2}MR^2\)) is mounted on a frictionless horizontal axle. A light string wrapped around the perimeter of the pulley is attached to a hanging block of mass \(m = 2.0\,\text{kg}\).

The system is released from rest. Assume the string does not slip on the pulley. Take \(g = 10\,\text{m/s}^2\).

a. Draw the free-body diagram for the block and the torque diagram for the pulley. b. Calculate the linear acceleration \(a\) of the descending block. c. Calculate the tension \(T\) in the string during the descent.

Show Step-by-Step Solution

Part a & b: Calculate linear acceleration \(a\):

  1. For the hanging mass \(m\) (translating downward): Apply Newton's Second Law: $\(\sum F_y = m g - T = m a \implies T = m(g - a)\)$

  2. For the pulley \(M\) (rotating clockwise): The string tension exerts a tangential torque at radius \(R\) (\(\theta = 90^\circ\)): $\(\tau_{\text{net}} = T \cdot R = I \alpha\)$

  3. No-slip condition: The linear acceleration of the string matches the tangential acceleration of the rim: $\(a = R \alpha \implies \alpha = \frac{a}{R}\)$

  4. Combine equations: Substitute \(I = \frac{1}{2}MR^2\) and \(\alpha = \frac{a}{R}\): $\(T \cdot R = \left(\frac{1}{2}M R^2\right) \left(\frac{a}{R}\right) = \frac{1}{2} M R a\)$ Divide through by \(R\): $\(T = \frac{1}{2} M a\)$

  5. Substitute \(T\) into the block's equation: $\(m g - \frac{1}{2} M a = m a\)$ $\(m g = \left(m + \frac{1}{2} M\right) a\)$ $\(a = \frac{m g}{m + \frac{1}{2} M} = \frac{(2.0)(10)}{2.0 + \frac{1}{2}(4.0)} = \frac{20}{2.0 + 2.0} = \frac{20}{4.0} = \mathbf{5.0\,\text{m/s}^2}\)$

Part c: Determine string tension \(T\):

Using \(T = \frac{1}{2} M a\):

\[T = \frac{1}{2}(4.0\,\text{kg})(5.0\,\text{m/s}^2) = \mathbf{10\,\text{N}}\]

(Notice that \(T = 10\,\text{N} < mg = 20\,\text{N}\), which is required for the hanging block to accelerate downward).

docs.title: Unit 6: Energy & Momentum of Rotating Systems
docs.text: Rotating bodies possess both kinetic energy distributed across their moving mass and angular momentum that remains conserved in the absence of net external torques.

docs.title: 6.1 Rotational Kinetic Energy & Work
docs.text:
For a rigid body rotating with angular velocity \(\omega\) about an axis:

\[K_{\text{rot}} = \frac{1}{2} I \omega^2\]

docs.title: Work Done by a Torque
docs.text:
A torque \(\tau\) acting through an angular displacement \(\Delta\theta\) does work on the rotating system:

\[W = \tau \Delta\theta\]

By the Work-Energy Theorem for Rotation:

\[W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K_{\text{rot}} = \frac{1}{2} I \omega_f^2 - \frac{1}{2} I \omega_i^2\]

docs.title: 6.2 Rolling Without Slipping
docs.text: When a symmetrical object (cylinder, sphere, hoop) of mass \(M\) and radius \(R\) rolls without slipping along a surface: - The point of contact with the ground is instantaneously at rest (\(v_{\text{contact}} = 0\)), held by static friction. - The translational center of mass speed and angular speed are coupled: $\(v_{\text{cm}} = R \omega\)$

docs.title: Total Mechanical Kinetic Energy
docs.text:
The total kinetic energy is partitioned into translational and rotational contributions:

\[K_{\text{total}} = K_{\text{trans}} + K_{\text{rot}} = \frac{1}{2} M v_{\text{cm}}^2 + \frac{1}{2} I_{\text{cm}} \omega^2\]

Writing \(I_{\text{cm}} = c M R^2\) (where \(c\) is the shape constant, e.g. \(c = 1/2\) for a disk, \(c = 2/5\) for a sphere):

\[K_{\text{total}} = \frac{1}{2} M v_{\text{cm}}^2 + \frac{1}{2}(c M R^2)\left(\frac{v_{\text{cm}}}{R}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{2} M v_{\text{cm}}^2(1 + c)\]

docs.title: 6.3 Angular Momentum
docs.text:
Angular momentum (\(\vec{L}\)) is the rotational analog of linear momentum:

  1. For a Rigid Extended Object Rotating about a Principal Axis: $\(L = I \omega\)$
  2. For a Point Particle of Mass \(m\) Moving at Velocity \(\vec{v}\) Relative to a Pivot: $\(L = r_\perp p = m v r \sin\theta\)$ where \(r_\perp\) is the perpendicular distance from the chosen origin to the particle's velocity vector line.

docs.title: 6.4 The Angular Impulse-Momentum Theorem
docs.text:
Newton's Second Law for rotation in terms of angular momentum:

\[\vec{\tau}_{\text{net}} = \frac{\Delta\vec{L}}{\Delta t} \implies \Delta\vec{L} = \vec{\tau}_{\text{net}} \Delta t\]

The angular impulse imparted by an external torque produces a change in the total angular momentum of the system.

docs.title: 6.5 Conservation of Angular Momentum
docs.text:
If the net external torque acting on a system about a chosen axis is zero (\(\sum \vec{\tau}_{\text{ext}} = 0\)):

\[\sum \vec{L}_i = \sum \vec{L}_f \iff I_i \omega_i = I_f \omega_f\]

docs.title: Key Physical Phenomenon: Changing Rotational Inertia
docs.text:
When an internal mechanism alters mass distribution (e.g., a spinning figure skater pulling their arms inward): - \(I\) decreases \(\implies \omega\) must increase to preserve \(L = I\omega\). - Kinetic energy is NOT conserved: \(K = \frac{L^2}{2I}\) increases because the skater's muscles perform positive work pulling the mass inward against centrifugal effects!

AP Exam Tip: The Great Incline Rolling Race

A classic AP Physics 1 question releases a solid sphere (\(I = \frac{2}{5}MR^2\)), a uniform disk (\(I = \frac{1}{2}MR^2\)), and a hollow hoop (\(I = MR^2\)) from rest at the top of an incline of height \(h\).

By energy conservation: $\(M g h = \frac{1}{2} M v^2(1 + c) \implies v = \sqrt{\frac{2gh}{1 + c}}\)$

  • Smaller \(c \implies\) less energy diverted to rotation \(\implies\) higher linear speed \(v\).
  • Finishing order: Solid Sphere (\(c = 0.40\)) wins first, followed by Disk (\(c = 0.50\)), and Hoop (\(c = 1.0\)) finishes last!
  • Notice: This result is completely independent of the mass \(M\) and radius \(R\)!

docs.title: 📝 Practice Problem & Solution
docs.text:
Practice Problem 6.1: Point Mass Striking a Pivoted Rod

A uniform thin rod of mass \(M = 3.0\,\text{kg}\) and length \(L = 0.80\,\text{m}\) is pivoted at its top end about a frictionless horizontal pin (\(I_{\text{rod}} = \frac{1}{3}ML^2\)). The rod hangs vertically at rest.

A small sticky clay blob of mass \(m = 0.50\,\text{kg}\) traveling horizontally with velocity \(v_0 = 12\,\text{m/s}\) strikes the very bottom tip of the rod and sticks to it.

a. Calculate the rotational inertia of the combined rod + clay system about the pivot immediately after impact. b. Using conservation of angular momentum about the pivot, calculate the initial angular velocity \(\omega\) of the system immediately following the collision.

Show Step-by-Step Solution

Part a: Rotational inertia of the composite system:

The composite rotational inertia about the pivot is the sum of the rod and the clay blob (treated as a point mass at distance \(L\)):

\[I_{\text{total}} = I_{\text{rod}} + I_{\text{clay}} = \frac{1}{3} M L^2 + m L^2 = \left(\frac{1}{3}M + m\right) L^2\]

Substitute the numerical values:

\[I_{\text{total}} = \left(\frac{1}{3}(3.0) + 0.50\right) (0.80)^2 = (1.0 + 0.50)(0.64) = (1.50)(0.64) = \mathbf{0.96\,\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2}\]

Part b: Angular velocity from conservation of angular momentum:

Choose the pivot as the origin. During the brief collision, external forces act at the pivot (\(r = 0\)), so the external torque about the pivot is zero (\(\tau_{\text{ext}} = 0\)). Angular momentum is conserved:

\[L_i = L_f\]

Before the collision, the rod is at rest. The moving clay blob has angular momentum:

\[L_i = r_\perp p = L(m v_0)\] \[L_i = (0.80\,\text{m})(0.50\,\text{kg})(12\,\text{m/s}) = (0.80)(6.0) = 4.8\,\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}\]

After the collision, the combined system rotates as a single rigid body with angular momentum:

\[L_f = I_{\text{total}} \omega\]

Set \(L_i = L_f\):

\[4.8 = 0.96 \omega\] \[\omega = \frac{4.8}{0.96} = \mathbf{5.0\,\text{rad/s}}\]

docs.title: Unit 7: Oscillations
docs.text: Oscillatory motion occurs when an object is displaced from a stable equilibrium position and experiences a linear restoring force that drives it back toward equilibrium.

docs.title: 7.1 Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM)
docs.text:
A system executes Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) if the restoring force is directly proportional to displacement and directed opposite to it:

\[F_{\text{net}} = -k x \implies m a = -k x \implies a = -\left(\frac{k}{m}\right) x = -\omega^2 x\]

where \(\omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{k}{m}}\) is the angular frequency (in rad/s).

docs.title: Kinematics of SHM
docs.text:
Assuming the oscillator is released from maximum displacement \(x = A\) at \(t = 0\):

\[x(t) = A \cos(\omega t)\] \[v(t) = \frac{dx}{dt} = -A\omega \sin(\omega t)\] \[a(t) = \frac{dv}{dt} = -A\omega^2 \cos(\omega t) = -\omega^2 x(t)\]
  • Maximum Speed (\(v_{\text{max}}\)): Occurs at the equilibrium position (\(x = 0\)): $\(v_{\text{max}} = A \omega\)$
  • Maximum Acceleration (\(a_{\text{max}}\)): Occurs at the turning points (\(x = \pm A\)): $\(a_{\text{max}} = A \omega^2\)$

docs.title: 7.2 Period and Frequency
docs.text:
• Period (\(T\)): The time required to complete one full cycle of oscillation (in seconds): $\(T = \frac{1}{f} = \frac{2\pi}{\omega}\)$
  • Frequency (\(f\)): The number of oscillations completed per second (in Hertz, \(\text{Hz} = \text{s}^{-1}\)): $\(f = \frac{1}{T} = \frac{\omega}{2\pi}\)$

docs.title: 1. Mass-Spring Oscillator
docs.text:
For a mass \(m\) attached to an ideal spring of force constant \(k\) (horizontal or vertical):

\[\omega = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}} \implies T_s = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}\]
  • Independent of: Amplitude (\(A\)) and local gravitational acceleration (\(g\)).

docs.title: 2. Simple Pendulum (Small Angle Approximation)
docs.text:
For a point mass \(m\) suspended from a string of length \(L\) in gravitational field \(g\):

\[\tau_{\text{net}} = -(mg\sin\theta) L \approx -mgL\theta \quad (\text{for } \theta \le 15^\circ)\] \[\omega = \sqrt{\frac{g}{L}} \implies T_p = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}\]
  • Independent of: Bob mass (\(m\)) and amplitude (\(\theta_0\), within small-angle regime).

docs.title: 7.4 Energy Transformations in SHM
docs.text:
In an ideal, undamped oscillator, mechanical energy continuously shifts between kinetic energy (\(K\)) and potential energy (\(U\)):

\[E_{\text{total}} = K + U = \frac{1}{2} m v^2 + \frac{1}{2} k x^2 = \text{constant}\]

At the turning points (\(x = \pm A, v = 0\)):

\[E_{\text{total}} = \frac{1}{2} k A^2\]

At the equilibrium position (\(x = 0, v = \pm v_{\text{max}}\)):

\[E_{\text{total}} = \frac{1}{2} m v_{\text{max}}^2\]

Equating the two expressions:

\[\frac{1}{2} m v_{\text{max}}^2 = \frac{1}{2} k A^2 \implies v_{\text{max}} = A \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}} = A \omega\]

AP Exam Trap: Gravity Does NOT Alter Vertical Spring Period

When a mass hangs vertically from a spring, gravity shifts the equilibrium position downward by \(\Delta y_0 = \frac{mg}{k}\).

However, because the restoring force relative to the new equilibrium is still linear (\(F_{\text{net}} = -k y'\)), the frequency and period are completely unchanged: $\(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}\)$

A vertical spring oscillating on Earth will oscillate with the exact same period if taken to the Moon or placed in a freely falling elevator!

docs.title: 📝 Practice Problem & Solution
docs.text:
Practice Problem 7.1: Energy and Kinematics of a Spring Oscillator

A block of mass \(m = 0.50\,\text{kg}\) on a frictionless horizontal surface is attached to a spring with \(k = 200\,\text{N/m}\). The block is pulled to \(x = +0.10\,\text{m}\) (\(10\,\text{cm}\)) and released from rest at \(t = 0\).

a. Calculate the period \(T\) and maximum speed \(v_{\text{max}}\) of the oscillation. b. Determine the speed of the block when its position is \(x = 0.06\,\text{m}\) (\(6\,\text{cm}\)). c. What fraction of the total mechanical energy is kinetic energy at \(x = 0.06\,\text{m}\)?

Show Step-by-Step Solution

Part a: Calculate period \(T\) and maximum speed \(v_{\text{max}}\):

Angular frequency:

\[\omega = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}} = \sqrt{\frac{200}{0.50}} = \sqrt{400} = 20\,\text{rad/s}\]

Period:

\[T = \frac{2\pi}{\omega} = \frac{2\pi}{20} = \frac{\pi}{10} \approx \mathbf{0.314\,\text{s}}\]

Maximum speed:

\[v_{\text{max}} = A \omega = (0.10\,\text{m})(20\,\text{rad/s}) = \mathbf{2.0\,\text{m/s}}\]

Part b: Speed at \(x = 0.06\,\text{m}\) using energy conservation:

Total mechanical energy:

\[E_{\text{total}} = \frac{1}{2} k A^2 = \frac{1}{2}(200)(0.10)^2 = 100(0.01) = 1.0\,\text{J}\]

At position \(x = 0.06\,\text{m}\):

\[U = \frac{1}{2} k x^2 = \frac{1}{2}(200)(0.06)^2 = 100(0.0036) = 0.36\,\text{J}\]

By conservation of energy:

\[K = E_{\text{total}} - U = 1.0\,\text{J} - 0.36\,\text{J} = 0.64\,\text{J}\]

Solve for \(v\):

\[\frac{1}{2} m v^2 = 0.64 \implies \frac{1}{2}(0.50) v^2 = 0.64 \implies 0.25 v^2 = 0.64\] \[v^2 = \frac{0.64}{0.25} = 2.56 \implies v = \sqrt{2.56} = \mathbf{1.6\,\text{m/s}}\]

Part c: Fraction of total energy in kinetic form:

\[\frac{K}{E_{\text{total}}} = \frac{0.64\,\text{J}}{1.0\,\text{J}} = 0.64 = \mathbf{64\%}\]

(Notice: \(\frac{K}{E} = 1 - \frac{x^2}{A^2} = 1 - \frac{0.06^2}{0.10^2} = 1 - 0.36 = 0.64\)).

docs.title: Unit 8: Fluids
docs.text: Fluids (liquids and gases) represent states of matter that yield continuously to shear stress and assume the shape of their containing boundaries.

docs.title: 8.1 Density & Pressure
docs.text:
• Density (\(\rho\)): Mass per unit volume (in \(\text{kg/m}^3\)): $\(\rho = \frac{m}{V}\)$ (For water at standard conditions, \(\rho_{\text{water}} = 1{,}000\,\text{kg/m}^3 = 1.0\,\text{g/cm}^3\)).

  • Pressure (\(P\)): Normal compressive force exerted per unit surface area (in Pascals, \(\text{Pa} = \text{N/m}^2\)): $\(P = \frac{F_\perp}{A}\)$ (Standard atmospheric pressure: \(P_{\text{atm}} = 1.013 \times 10^5\,\text{Pa} \approx 101\,\text{kPa}\)).

docs.title: 8.2 Hydrostatic Pressure & Pascal's Principle
docs.text:
For an incompressible fluid of uniform density \(\rho\) at rest, pressure increases linearly with vertical depth \(h\):

\[P = P_0 + \rho g h\]

where: - \(P_0\) is the pressure at the liquid surface (often \(P_{\text{atm}}\)). - \(\rho g h\) is the hydrostatic pressure contributed by the fluid column. - Gauge Pressure (\(P_g\)): The difference between absolute pressure and atmospheric pressure: $\(P_g = P - P_{\text{atm}} = \rho g h\)$

docs.title: Pascal's Principle
docs.text:
An external pressure applied to an enclosed, incompressible fluid is transmitted undiminished to every portion of the fluid and container walls:

\[\Delta P_1 = \Delta P_2 \implies \frac{F_1}{A_1} = \frac{F_2}{A_2} \implies F_2 = F_1 \left(\frac{A_2}{A_1}\right)\]

docs.title: 8.3 Archimedes' Principle & Buoyancy
docs.text:
An object wholly or partially immersed in a fluid experiences an upward buoyant force (\(\vec{F}_b\)) equal to the weight of the fluid displaced by the object:

\[F_b = m_{\text{fluid, displaced}} \, g = \rho_{\text{fluid}} V_{\text{submerged}} g\]

docs.title: Floating & Sinking Criteria
docs.text:
1. Fully Submerged Object: $\(F_{\text{net}} = F_b - F_g = \rho_{\text{fluid}} V g - \rho_{\text{object}} V g = (\rho_{\text{fluid}} - \rho_{\text{object}}) V g\)$
  2. Sinks if \(\rho_{\text{object}} > \rho_{\text{fluid}}\).
  3. Suspended if \(\rho_{\text{object}} = \rho_{\text{fluid}}\).
  4. Floating Object in Static Equilibrium (\(\sum F_y = 0\)): $\(F_b = F_g \implies \rho_{\text{fluid}} V_{\text{submerged}} g = \rho_{\text{object}} V_{\text{total}} g\)$ $\(\frac{V_{\text{submerged}}}{V_{\text{total}}} = \frac{\rho_{\text{object}}}{\rho_{\text{fluid}}}\)$ (The fraction submerged equals the ratio of object density to fluid density).

docs.title: 8.4 Fluid Dynamics: The Continuity Equation
docs.text:
For an ideal fluid (incompressible, non-viscous, laminar streamline flow), mass conservation dictates that the volumetric flow rate (\(Q\)) remains constant along a pipe of varying cross-sectional area:

\[Q = A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2 = \text{constant}\]

where \(A\) is the cross-sectional area and \(v\) is the average fluid velocity: - As the pipe narrows (\(A\) decreases), fluid speed \(v\) must increase proportionally: $\(v_2 = v_1 \left(\frac{A_1}{A_2}\right)\)$

docs.title: 8.5 Bernoulli's Equation
docs.text:
Bernoulli's equation represents the work-energy theorem applied to a continuous fluid streamline:

\[P_1 + \frac{1}{2}\rho v_1^2 + \rho g y_1 = P_2 + \frac{1}{2}\rho v_2^2 + \rho g y_2 = \text{constant}\]

where: - \(P\) is the static pressure energy density. - \(\frac{1}{2}\rho v^2\) is the kinetic energy density of fluid motion. - \(\rho g y\) is the gravitational potential energy density.

docs.title: Torricelli's Law
docs.text:
For a large open tank of liquid with a small drain hole at depth \(h\) below the surface (\(A_{\text{tank}} \gg A_{\text{hole}} \implies v_{\text{surface}} \approx 0\) and \(P_{\text{surface}} = P_{\text{hole}} = P_{\text{atm}}\)):

\[v = \sqrt{2gh}\]

AP Exam Tip: The Venturi Effect (Narrow Pipe Means LOWER Pressure)

A common misconception is believing that when water or air rushes into a narrow constriction, pressure increases because the fluid is "squeezed".

In reality, by the continuity equation, the fluid must accelerate to a higher velocity (\(v_2 > v_1\)).

By Bernoulli's equation at horizontal height (\(y_1 = y_2\)): $\(P_1 + \frac{1}{2}\rho v_1^2 = P_2 + \frac{1}{2}\rho v_2^2\)$

Because the kinetic energy density \(\frac{1}{2}\rho v^2\) increases, the static pressure \(P\) must decrease: $\(v_2 > v_1 \implies P_2 < P_1\)$

This static pressure reduction explains lift in airplane wings, atomizer sprayers, and the Venturi flow meter.

docs.title: 📝 Practice Problem & Solution
docs.text:
Practice Problem 8.1: Buoyancy and Apparent Weight

A solid metal sculpture of unknown composition has a mass of \(m = 12.0\,\text{kg}\). When the sculpture is completely submerged in a vat of water (\(\rho_{\text{water}} = 1{,}000\,\text{kg/m}^3\)), a spring scale attached to the sculpture reads an apparent weight of \(F_{\text{scale}} = 75.0\,\text{N}\). Take \(g = 10\,\text{m/s}^2\).

a. Calculate the magnitude of the buoyant force exerted on the submerged sculpture. b. Determine the volume \(V\) of the sculpture. c. Calculate the density \(\rho_{\text{metal}}\) of the sculpture and state whether it would float in liquid mercury (\(\rho_{\text{mercury}} = 13{,}600\,\text{kg/m}^3\)).

Show Step-by-Step Solution

Part a: Calculate the buoyant force:

Draw the vertical forces on the submerged sculpture in static equilibrium: - Upward scale tension: \(F_{\text{scale}} = 75.0\,\text{N}\) - Upward buoyant force: \(F_b\) - Downward true weight: \(F_g = mg = (12.0\,\text{kg})(10\,\text{m/s}^2) = 120.0\,\text{N}\)

Apply Newton's First Law (\(\sum F_y = 0\)):

\[F_{\text{scale}} + F_b - F_g = 0\] \[F_b = F_g - F_{\text{scale}} = 120.0\,\text{N} - 75.0\,\text{N} = \mathbf{45.0\,\text{N}}\]

Part b: Determine the volume of the sculpture:

By Archimedes' Principle:

\[F_b = \rho_{\text{water}} V_{\text{submerged}} g\]

Since the sculpture is completely submerged, \(V = V_{\text{submerged}}\):

\[45.0\,\text{N} = (1{,}000\,\text{kg/m}^3)(10\,\text{m/s}^2) V = 10{,}000 V\] \[V = \frac{45.0}{10{,}000} = \mathbf{0.0045\,\text{m}^3} = 4.5 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{m}^3 \quad (4.5\,\text{liters})\]

Part c: Determine density of the sculpture:

\[\rho_{\text{metal}} = \frac{m}{V} = \frac{12.0\,\text{kg}}{0.0045\,\text{m}^3} \approx \mathbf{2{,}667\,\text{kg/m}^3}\]

(This is approximately the density of solid aluminum, \(\approx 2{,}700\,\text{kg/m}^3\)).

Floating in mercury: Since \(\rho_{\text{metal}} = 2{,}667\,\text{kg/m}^3 < \rho_{\text{mercury}} = 13{,}600\,\text{kg/m}^3\), the sculpture will easily float in mercury, with:

\[\frac{V_{\text{submerged}}}{V} = \frac{2{,}667}{13{,}600} \approx 0.196 = \mathbf{19.6\%} \text{ submerged}\]

docs.title: 🎯 High-Yield AP Exam Recommendations
docs.text:
1. Precision in Justifications: Whenever asked to justify that a function is increasing or concave up, explicitly compute the Average Rate of Change (AROC) across consecutive intervals.
  2. Limit Notation for End Behavior: Always express horizontal asymptotes using standard limit notation: \(\lim_{x \to \infty} f(x) = L \quad \text{and} \quad \lim_{x \to -\infty} f(x) = L\)
  3. Factoring First: When analyzing rational functions, factor completely to immediately distinguish removable discontinuities (holes) from infinite discontinuities (vertical asymptotes).
  4. Logarithmic Domains: Always check for extraneous roots in candidate solutions to logarithmic equations (\(x > 0\)).

docs.title: 1.1 Average Rate of Change (AROC)
docs.text:
The Average Rate of Change of a function \(f\) over the closed interval \([a, b]\) represents the slope of the secant line passing through \((a, f(a))\) and \((b, f(b))\):

\[\text{AROC}_{[a, b]} = \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x} = \frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}\]

docs.title: Concavity via Rates of Change
docs.text:
The shape of a graph can be deduced by examining consecutive rates of change over equal intervals \([x_1, x_2]\) and \([x_2, x_3]\) (where \(x_2 - x_1 = x_3 - x_2\)):

  • Concave Up: The average rates of change are increasing: $\(\text{AROC}_{[x_1, x_2]} < \text{AROC}_{[x_2, x_3]}\)$
  • Concave Down: The average rates of change are decreasing: $\(\text{AROC}_{[x_1, x_2]} > \text{AROC}_{[x_2, x_3]}\)$

docs.title: 1.2 Polynomial Functions & End Behavior
docs.text:
For a general polynomial function of degree \(n\):

\[P(x) = a_n x^n + a_{n-1} x^{n-1} + \dots + a_1 x + a_0 \quad (a_n \neq 0)\]

The global end behavior is dictated entirely by its leading term \(a_n x^n\):

\[\lim_{x \to \infty} P(x) = \lim_{x \to \infty} a_n x^n \quad \text{and} \quad \lim_{x \to -\infty} P(x) = \lim_{x \to -\infty} a_n x^n\]

docs.title: 1.3 Rational Functions & Asymptotes
docs.text: Let \(R(x) = \frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}\) where \(P(x)\) and \(Q(x)\) are polynomials.

docs.title: Removable vs. Vertical Asymptotes
docs.text: If \(x - c\) is a factor of both \(P(x)\) and \(Q(x)\): - If the multiplicity of \((x - c)\) in \(P(x)\) is greater than or equal to its multiplicity in \(Q(x)\), \(x = c\) corresponds to a hole at \(\left(c, \lim_{x \to c} R(x)\right)\). - If the multiplicity in \(Q(x)\) is strictly greater, \(x = c\) produces a vertical asymptote: $\(\lim_{x \to c^+} R(x) = \pm\infty \quad \text{or} \quad \lim_{x \to c^-} R(x) = \pm\infty\)$

docs.title: Horizontal Asymptotes Degree Test
docs.text:
Comparing the degree of the numerator \(n = \deg(P)\) with the degree of the denominator \(m = \deg(Q)\):

\[\lim_{x \to \pm\infty} \frac{a_n x^n + \dots}{b_m x^m + \dots} = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } n < m \implies y = 0 \\ \dfrac{a_n}{b_m} & \text{if } n = m \implies y = \dfrac{a_n}{b_m} \\ \pm\infty & \text{if } n > m \implies \text{No Horizontal Asymptote} \end{cases}\]

AP Exam Tip: Justifying Removable Discontinuities

On Free-Response Questions (FRQs), never simply write "the factor cancels out so it's a hole". You must state:

  1. The denominator \(Q(c) = 0\), so \(R(c)\) is undefined.
  2. The two-sided limit exists: \(\lim_{x \to c} R(x) = L \in \mathbb{R}\).
  3. Therefore, \(R\) possesses a removable discontinuity at \((c, L)\).

docs.title: 📝 Practice Problem & Solution
docs.text:
Practice Problem 1.1: Rational Function Analysis

Consider the rational function:

\[f(x) = \frac{2x^2 - 8}{x^2 - 5x + 6}\]

a. Determine the coordinates of any holes in the graph of \(f(x)\). b. Identify all vertical and horizontal asymptotes. Use limit notation to justify your answers.

Show Step-by-Step Solution

Step 1: Completely factor the numerator and denominator:

\[f(x) = \frac{2(x^2 - 4)}{(x - 2)(x - 3)} = \frac{2(x - 2)(x + 2)}{(x - 2)(x - 3)}\]

Step 2: Identify and evaluate holes (removable discontinuities):

The common factor is \((x - 2)\). For all \(x \neq 2\):

\[\tilde{f}(x) = \frac{2(x + 2)}{x - 3}\]

Evaluating the limit as \(x \to 2\):

\[\lim_{x \to 2} f(x) = \frac{2(2 + 2)}{2 - 3} = \frac{8}{-1} = -8\]

Therefore, there is a hole at \((2, -8)\).

Step 3: Vertical Asymptotes:

The remaining non-canceled denominator factor is \((x - 3)\):

\[\lim_{x \to 3^+} f(x) = \frac{2(3 + 2)}{3^+ - 3} = \frac{10}{0^+} = +\infty\]

Thus, \(x = 3\) is a vertical asymptote.

Step 4: Horizontal Asymptotes:

Both numerator and denominator have degree \(2\) (\(n = m = 2\)). Evaluating end behavior:

\[\lim_{x \to \pm\infty} f(x) = \lim_{x \to \pm\infty} \frac{2x^2}{x^2} = 2\]

Thus, \(y = 2\) is a horizontal asymptote.

docs.title: 2.1 Arithmetic vs. Geometric Sequences
docs.text:
Sequences serve as the discrete foundation for continuous linear and exponential functions:

Feature Arithmetic Sequence Geometric Sequence Recursive Definition \(a_n = a_{n-1} + d\) \(g_n = g_{n-1} \cdot r\) Explicit Formula \(a_n = a_1 + (n - 1)d\) \(g_n = g_1 \cdot r^{n-1}\) Continuous Analogy Linear function: \(f(x) = mx + b\) Exponential function: \(f(x) = a \cdot b^x\) Rate of Change Constant additive difference (\(d\)) Constant multiplicative factor (\(r\))

docs.title: 2.2 Exponential Function Modeling
docs.text:
An exponential function changes by equal factors over equal intervals:

\[f(x) = a \cdot b^x = a(1 + r)^x\]

where: - \(a = f(0)\) is the initial value (non-zero). - \(b > 0\) with \(b \neq 1\) is the base / growth factor. - \(r = b - 1\) is the growth or decay rate per unit input.

docs.title: Continuous Compounding & Natural Base \(e\)
docs.text:
When compounding occurs continuously, Euler's number \(e = \lim_{n \to \infty} \left(1 + \frac{1}{n}\right)^n \approx 2.71828\dots\) emerges:

\[A(t) = P \cdot e^{kt}\]
  • If \(k > 0\), the quantity experiences continuous growth.
  • If \(k < 0\), the quantity experiences continuous decay.

docs.title: Half-Life and Doubling Time
docs.text:
For radioactive decay with half-life \(t_{1/2}\), the remaining quantity is modeled as:

\[N(t) = N_0 \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{t / t_{1/2}} = N_0 e^{-kt} \quad \text{where} \quad k = \frac{\ln 2}{t_{1/2}}\]

Similarly, for doubling time \(t_d\):

\[P(t) = P_0 (2)^{t / t_d} = P_0 e^{kt} \quad \text{where} \quad k = \frac{\ln 2}{t_d}\]

docs.title: 2.3 Composition, Inverses, & Logarithmic Functions
docs.text:
A logarithm is defined as the inverse of an exponential function:

\[y = \log_b(x) \iff b^y = x \quad (b > 0, \; b \neq 1, \; x > 0)\]
  • Domain: \((0, \infty)\)
  • Range: \((-\infty, \infty)\)
  • Vertical Asymptote: \(x = 0\) (with \(\lim_{x \to 0^+} \log_b(x) = -\infty\) for \(b > 1\))

docs.title: Essential Logarithmic Properties
docs.text: \[\log_b(xy) = \log_b(x) + \log_b(y) \quad \text{(Product Property)}\] \[\log_b\left(\frac{x}{y}\right) = \log_b(x) - \log_b(y) \quad \text{(Quotient Property)}\] \[\log_b(x^k) = k \cdot \log_b(x) \quad \text{(Power Property)}\] \[\log_b(a) = \frac{\ln a}{\ln b} = \frac{\log_{10} a}{\log_{10} b} \quad \text{(Change of Base Formula)}\]

docs.title: 2.4 Semi-Log Plots & Data Linearization
docs.text:
When exponential data \((x, y)\) is plotted on a semi-log plot (where the vertical axis is scaled logarithmically):

Given \(y = a \cdot b^x\), take the natural logarithm of both sides:

\[\ln(y) = \ln(a \cdot b^x) = \ln(a) + \ln(b^x)\] \[\ln(y) = (\ln b) \cdot x + \ln(a)\]

This matches standard slope-intercept form \(Y = m x + C\): - The dependent variable is \(Y = \ln(y)\). - The slope of the line is \(m = \ln(b) \implies b = e^m\). - The vertical intercept is \(C = \ln(a) \implies a = e^C\).

AP Exam Trap: Checking for Extraneous Solutions

When solving logarithmic equations, combining terms using the product or quotient rules can introduce extraneous solutions that violate the strict domain requirement \(x > 0\).

For example, in \(\log_2(x) + \log_2(x - 2) = 3\): $\(\log_2(x(x - 2)) = 3 \implies x^2 - 2x = 8 \implies x^2 - 2x - 8 = 0\)$ $\((x - 4)(x + 2) = 0 \implies x = 4 \quad \text{or} \quad x = -2\)$

You must reject \(x = -2\) because \(\log_2(-2)\) is undefined in the real numbers. Always check candidate roots in the original unsimplified equation.

docs.title: 📝 Practice Problem & Solution
docs.text:
Practice Problem 2.1: Continuous Modeling & Semi-Log Linearization

A biological culture of bacteria is treated with an antibiotic. The population \(P(t)\) is modeled by an exponential decay function \(P(t) = P_0 e^{-kt}\), where \(t\) is measured in hours.

At \(t = 0\), the culture contains \(8{,}000\) bacteria. After \(3\) hours, the population has decreased to \(1{,}000\) bacteria.

a. Determine the exact continuous decay rate \(k\) and write the complete formula for \(P(t)\). b. Express \(\ln(P(t))\) as a linear function of \(t\). State the slope and vertical intercept of the resulting line. c. Determine the half-life of the bacteria under this antibiotic treatment.

Show Step-by-Step Solution

Part a: Determine \(P_0\) and the decay constant \(k\):

The initial condition gives \(P_0 = P(0) = 8{,}000\).

At \(t = 3\), \(P(3) = 1{,}000\):

\[1{,}000 = 8{,}000 \, e^{-3k}\]

Divide both sides by \(8{,}000\):

\[\frac{1}{8} = e^{-3k}\]

Take the natural logarithm of both sides:

\[\ln\left(\frac{1}{8}\right) = -3k \implies -\ln(8) = -3k\]

Since \(8 = 2^3\), \(\ln(8) = 3\ln(2)\):

\[k = \frac{3\ln(2)}{3} = \ln(2) \approx 0.6931\,\text{hr}^{-1}\]

Therefore, the exact population model is:

\[P(t) = 8{,}000 \, e^{-(\ln 2)t} = 8{,}000 \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^t\]

Part b: Linearization on a Semi-Log Plot:

Take the natural logarithm of both sides:

\[\ln(P(t)) = \ln\left(8{,}000 \, e^{-kt}\right) = \ln(8{,}000) + \ln\left(e^{-kt}\right)\] \[\ln(P(t)) = -kt + \ln(8{,}000) = -(\ln 2)t + \ln(8{,}000)\]
  • Slope: \(m = -k = -\ln(2) \approx -0.6931\)
  • Vertical Intercept: \(C = \ln(8{,}000) \approx 8.987\)

Part c: Determine the Half-Life:

The half-life \(t_{1/2}\) is the time required for the population to reach \(\frac{1}{2}P_0 = 4{,}000\):

\[4{,}000 = 8{,}000 \, e^{-(\ln 2) t_{1/2}} \implies \frac{1}{2} = e^{-(\ln 2) t_{1/2}}\] \[-\ln(2) = -(\ln 2) t_{1/2} \implies t_{1/2} = \mathbf{1\,\text{hour}}\]

(Notice this is immediate from the base-2 simplified model \(P(t) = 8{,}000(1/2)^t\), where \(t\) is in hours).

docs.title: 3.1 Radian Measure & The Unit Circle
docs.text:
An angle of \(\theta\) radians subtends an arc length \(s\) equal to \(\theta\) on a circle of radius \(r = 1\):

\[\theta = \frac{s}{r} \implies s = r\theta\]

On the unit circle (\(x^2 + y^2 = 1\)), the coordinates of the terminal ray point at angle \(\theta\) define the circular functions:

\[\cos\theta = x, \quad \sin\theta = y, \quad \tan\theta = \frac{y}{x} = \frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} \quad (x \neq 0)\] \[\sec\theta = \frac{1}{\cos\theta}, \quad \csc\theta = \frac{1}{\sin\theta}, \quad \cot\theta = \frac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\]

docs.title: Core Pythagorean Identities
docs.text: \[\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1\] \[\tan^2\theta + 1 = \sec^2\theta\] \[1 + \cot^2\theta = \csc^2\theta\]

docs.title: 3.2 Sinusoidal Modeling & Transformations
docs.text:
A sinusoidal function models periodic behavior using the general form:

\[f(t) = a \sin(b(t - c)) + d \quad \text{or} \quad f(t) = a \cos(b(t - c)) + d\]

where: - Amplitude: \(|a| = \dfrac{\text{Maximum} - \text{Minimum}}{2}\) - Midline (Vertical Shift): \(y = d = \dfrac{\text{Maximum} + \text{Minimum}}{2}\) - Period (\(T\)): The length of one complete cycle: $\(T = \frac{2\pi}{|b|} \iff |b| = \frac{2\pi}{T}\)$ - Frequency (\(f\)): \(f = \dfrac{1}{T} = \dfrac{|b|}{2\pi}\) - Phase Shift (Horizontal Shift): \(c\) (shifts right if \(c > 0\), left if \(c < 0\))

docs.title: 3.3 Inverse Trigonometric Functions
docs.text:
Because trigonometric functions are periodic, their domains must be restricted to standard principal branches so that they become one-to-one (invertible):

Function Notation Restricted Domain of \(f\) (Range of \(f^{-1}\)) Domain of \(f^{-1}\) Arcsine \(y = \arcsin(x) = \sin^{-1}(x)\) \(\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\) \([-1, 1]\) Arccosine \(y = \arccos(x) = \cos^{-1}(x)\) \([0, \pi]\) \([-1, 1]\) Arctangent \(y = \arctan(x) = \tan^{-1}(x)\) \(\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\) \((-\infty, \infty)\)

docs.title: 3.4 Double-Angle & Sum/Difference Identities
docs.text: \[\sin(2\theta) = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta\] \[\cos(2\theta) = \cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta = 2\cos^2\theta - 1 = 1 - 2\sin^2\theta\] \[\tan(2\theta) = \frac{2\tan\theta}{1 - \tan^2\theta}\]

docs.title: 3.5 Polar Coordinates & Complex Plane
docs.text: In the polar coordinate system, points are designated by \((r, \theta)\), where \(r\) is the directed radial distance from the pole (origin) and \(\theta\) is the angle from the polar axis.

docs.title: Conversion Formulas
docs.text: \[\begin{aligned} x &= r\cos\theta, & y &= r\sin\theta \\ r^2 &= x^2 + y^2, & \tan\theta &= \frac{y}{x} \quad (x \neq 0) \end{aligned}\]

docs.title: Complex Numbers in Polar (Trigonometric) Form
docs.text:
A complex number \(z = x + i y\) can be written in polar form with modulus \(r = |z| = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\) and argument \(\theta = \operatorname{arg}(z)\):

\[z = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta) = r e^{i\theta}\]

By De Moivre's Theorem, for any integer \(n\):

\[z^n = [r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)]^n = r^n(\cos(n\theta) + i\sin(n\theta))\]

AP Exam Tip: Interpreting Negative Radii in Polar Coordinates

In polar coordinates \((r, \theta)\), if \(r < 0\), the point is plotted by first rotating by \(\theta\), and then projecting a distance \(|r|\) in the opposite direction (along the ray \(\theta + \pi\)).

Therefore, the polar point: $\(\left(-3, \; \frac{\pi}{4}\right) \quad \text{is identical to} \quad \left(3, \; \frac{5\pi}{4}\right)\)$ In Cartesian coordinates: $\(x = -3\cos(\pi/4) = -\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}, \quad y = -3\sin(\pi/4) = -\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}\)$

docs.title: 📝 Practice Problem & Solution
docs.text:
Practice Problem 3.1: Modeling Periodic Ferris Wheel Motion

A giant Ferris wheel with a diameter of \(50\,\text{m}\) completes one full counterclockwise revolution every \(4\,\text{minutes}\). Passengers board the wheel at the lowest point, which is \(2\,\text{m}\) above the ground.

Assume a passenger boards at time \(t = 0\,\text{minutes}\).

a. Determine the amplitude, midline, and period of the passenger's height function \(h(t)\). b. Construct a sinusoidal function of the form \(h(t) = a\cos(b(t - c)) + d\) modeling the height \(h(t)\) in meters at time \(t\) in minutes. c. Find the first two positive times \(t > 0\) when the passenger is exactly \(40\,\text{m}\) above the ground.

Show Step-by-Step Solution

Part a: Determine geometric parameters: - Diameter \(= 50\,\text{m} \implies \text{Radius } R = 25\,\text{m}\). - Minimum height: \(h_{\text{min}} = 2\,\text{m}\). - Maximum height: \(h_{\text{max}} = 2 + 50 = 52\,\text{m}\). - Amplitude: \(a = \frac{h_{\text{max}} - h_{\text{min}}}{2} = \frac{52 - 2}{2} = \mathbf{25\,\text{m}}\). - Midline: \(d = \frac{h_{\text{max}} + h_{\text{min}}}{2} = \frac{52 + 2}{2} = \mathbf{27\,\text{m}}\). - Period: \(T = \mathbf{4\,\text{minutes}}\).

Part b: Formulate the cosine model:

The frequency parameter \(b\) is:

\[b = \frac{2\pi}{T} = \frac{2\pi}{4} = \frac{\pi}{2}\]

Since the passenger begins at the absolute minimum at \(t = 0\) (\(h(0) = 2\)), we can use an inverted cosine model (\(a = -25\)) with zero phase shift (\(c = 0\)):

\[h(t) = -25\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}t\right) + 27\]

Part c: Solve for \(h(t) = 40\,\text{m}\):

\[-25\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}t\right) + 27 = 40\] \[-25\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}t\right) = 13 \implies \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}t\right) = -\frac{13}{25} = -0.52\]

Take the principal inverse cosine:

\[\theta_1 = \arccos(-0.52) \approx 2.1179\,\text{radians}\]

By the symmetry of the cosine function on \([0, 2\pi]\), the second angle in the first cycle is:

\[\theta_2 = 2\pi - \theta_1 \approx 6.2832 - 2.1179 = 4.1653\,\text{radians}\]

Now solve for \(t = \frac{2}{\pi}\theta\):

\[t_1 = \frac{2}{\pi}(2.1179) \approx \mathbf{1.348\,\text{minutes}}\] \[t_2 = \frac{2}{\pi}(4.1653) \approx \mathbf{2.652\,\text{minutes}}\]

docs.title: 4.1 Parametric Functions
docs.text:
A parametric curve defines both the horizontal and vertical coordinates independently in terms of an auxiliary parameter (often time \(t\)):

\[\begin{cases} x = x(t) \\ y = y(t) \end{cases} \quad \text{for } t \in [t_{\text{min}}, t_{\text{max}}]\]

docs.title: Eliminating the Parameter
docs.text: To convert parametric equations into a single rectangular relationship \(y = f(x)\) or \(F(x, y) = 0\): 1. Algebraic Substitution: Solve for \(t\) in one equation (e.g., \(t = g(x)\)) and substitute into the second equation: \(y = y(g(x))\). 2. Trigonometric Elimination: When expressions involve sine and cosine, isolate the trig terms and apply the Pythagorean identity: $\(\left(\frac{x - h}{a}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{y - k}{b}\right)^2 = \cos^2 t + \sin^2 t = 1\)$

docs.title: 4.2 Conic Sections in Standard Form
docs.text:
Conic sections are implicit second-degree algebraic curves formed by intersecting a double cone with a plane:

Conic Section Standard Equation (Horizontal Major/Transverse Axis) Key Geometric Features Parabola \((y - k)^2 = 4p(x - h)\) Vertex \((h, k)\); Focus \((h+p, k)\); Directrix \(x = h - p\) Ellipse \(\dfrac{(x - h)^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{(y - k)^2}{b^2} = 1 \quad (a > b)\) Center \((h, k)\); Foci \((h \pm c, k)\) where \(c^2 = a^2 - b^2\) Hyperbola \(\dfrac{(x - h)^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{(y - k)^2}{b^2} = 1\) Center \((h, k)\); Foci \((h \pm c, k)\) where \(c^2 = a^2 + b^2\); Asymptotes \(y - k = \pm \frac{b}{a}(x - h)\)

docs.title: 4.3 Vectors in Two Dimensions
docs.text:
A vector \(\vec{v}\) represents a directed line segment possessing both magnitude (length) and direction:

\[\vec{v} = \langle v_x, v_y \rangle = v_x \hat{i} + v_y \hat{j}\]
  • Magnitude (Norm): \(\|\vec{v}\| = \sqrt{v_x^2 + v_y^2}\)
  • Direction Angle (\(\theta\)): \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{v_y}{v_x} \implies \vec{v} = \langle \|\vec{v}\|\cos\theta, \; \|\vec{v}\|\sin\theta \rangle\)
  • Unit Vector: \(\hat{u} = \dfrac{\vec{v}}{\|\vec{v}\|}\)

docs.title: The Dot Product & Orthogonality
docs.text:
The dot product of vectors \(\vec{u} = \langle u_1, u_2 \rangle\) and \(\vec{v} = \langle v_1, v_2 \rangle\) is an algebraic scalar:

\[\vec{u} \cdot \vec{v} = u_1 v_1 + u_2 v_2 = \|\vec{u}\| \|\vec{v}\| \cos\theta\] \[\cos\theta = \frac{\vec{u} \cdot \vec{v}}{\|\vec{u}\| \|\vec{v}\|}\] \[\vec{u} \perp \vec{v} \iff \vec{u} \cdot \vec{v} = 0 \quad (\text{Orthogonality Criterion})\]

docs.title: 4.4 Matrices & Planar Transformations
docs.text:
A \(2 \times 2\) matrix \(M = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}\) maps points \((x, y)\) in the plane to new coordinates \((x', y')\):

\[\begin{pmatrix} x' \\ y' \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} ax + by \\ cx + dy \end{pmatrix}\]
  • Determinant: \(\det(M) = ad - bc\). The determinant measures the area scaling factor under the transformation. If \(\det(M) < 0\), orientation is reversed (reflection).
  • Matrix Inverse: If \(\det(M) \neq 0\): $\(M^{-1} = \frac{1}{ad - bc} \begin{pmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{pmatrix}\)$

docs.title: Geometric Transformation Matrices
docs.text:
\[\text{Counterclockwise Rotation by } \theta: \quad R_\theta = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{pmatrix}\] \[\text{Reflection over } x\text{-axis}: \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \text{Reflection over } y = x: \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\] \[\text{Horizontal & Vertical Scaling}: \begin{pmatrix} k_x & 0 \\ 0 & k_y \end{pmatrix}\]

AP Exam Trap: Domain and Orientation of Parametric Curves

When eliminating a parameter, always verify whether the parameter interval restricts the resulting Cartesian domain or range.

For instance, if \(x(t) = t^2\) and \(y(t) = 2t\) for \(t \in \mathbb{R}\): Substituting \(t = y/2\) yields \(x = (y/2)^2 = y^2/4\).

However, because \(x(t) = t^2 \ge 0\), the curve is strictly the portion of the parabola in the right half-plane (\(x \ge 0\)). Always specify restricted domains when eliminating parameters!

docs.title: 📝 Practice Problem & Solution
docs.text:
Practice Problem 4.1: Vector Orthogonality & Matrix Transformation

Let vectors \(\vec{u} = \langle 3, -4 \rangle\) and \(\vec{v} = \langle 8, k \rangle\).

a. Determine the value of scalar \(k\) such that \(\vec{u}\) and \(\vec{v}\) are orthogonal. b. A linear transformation is given by matrix \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ -1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}\). Calculate \(\det(A)\) and determine the inverse matrix \(A^{-1}\). c. Use \(A^{-1}\) to solve the linear system: $\(\begin{aligned} 2x + y &= 7 \\ -x + 3y &= 7 \end{aligned}\)$

Show Step-by-Step Solution

Part a: Solve for \(k\) using the dot product condition:

Two vectors are orthogonal if and only if their dot product equals zero:

\[\vec{u} \cdot \vec{v} = (3)(8) + (-4)(k) = 0\] \[24 - 4k = 0 \implies 4k = 24 \implies k = \mathbf{6}\]

Part b: Compute \(\det(A)\) and \(A^{-1}\):

\[\det(A) = ad - bc = (2)(3) - (1)(-1) = 6 - (-1) = \mathbf{7}\]

Since \(\det(A) = 7 \neq 0\), the inverse exists:

\[A^{-1} = \frac{1}{\det(A)} \begin{pmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{7} \begin{pmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{3}{7} & -\dfrac{1}{7} \\ \dfrac{1}{7} & \dfrac{2}{7} \end{pmatrix}\]

Part c: Solve the matrix equation \(A X = B\):

The system can be written in matrix form as:

\[\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ -1 & 3 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 7 \\ 7 \end{pmatrix}\]

Multiply both sides by \(A^{-1}\):

\[\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} = A^{-1} \begin{pmatrix} 7 \\ 7 \end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{7} \begin{pmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 7 \\ 7 \end{pmatrix}\]

Perform the matrix-vector multiplication:

\[\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{7} \begin{pmatrix} (3)(7) + (-1)(7) \\ (1)(7) + (2)(7) \end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{7} \begin{pmatrix} 21 - 7 \\ 7 + 14 \end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{7} \begin{pmatrix} 14 \\ 21 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{2} \\ \mathbf{3} \end{pmatrix}\]

Thus, \(x = 2\) and \(y = 3\). (Check: \(2(2) + 3 = 7\) and \(-2 + 3(3) = 7\)).

• General Transformation Model: \(g(x) = a \cdot f(b(x - h)) + k\).
  • Vertical Transformations (Outside the Function):
    • \(a > 1\): Vertical stretch by factor \(|a|\); \(0 < a < 1\): Vertical compression.

    • \(k\): Vertical shift (up if \(k > 0\), down if \(k < 0\)).
  • Horizontal Transformations (Inside the Function):
    • \(b > 1\): Horizontal compression by factor \(\frac{1}{|b|}\); \(0 < b < 1\): Horizontal stretch.
    • \(b < 0\): Reflection across the \(y\)-axis.
    • \(h\): Horizontal shift (right if \(h > 0\), left if \(h < 0\)).

\[g(x) = a \cdot f\big(b(x - h)\big) + k\]

docs.text:
• Average Rate of Change (AROC): Measures the net change in output per unit change in input across a closed interval \([a, b]\).
  • Geometric Meaning: AROC equals the slope of the secant line intersecting \((a, f(a))\) and \((b, f(b))\).
  • Units of Rate of Change: Units are always \(\dfrac{\text{units of } f(x)}{\text{units of } x}\) (e.g., meters per second, degrees Celsius per hour).

docs.title: 📐 Essential Formulas & Definitions
docs.text:
Average Rate of Change (AROC):

\[\text{AROC}_{[a, b]} = \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x} = \frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}\]

AP Exam Tip

Always specify correct dimensional units whenever computing AROC in a contextual problem. Missing units is one of the most common causes of point deduction on AP exams!

docs.text:
• Linear Functions: Characterized by a constant average rate of change over equal intervals: \(\text{AROC} = m = \text{constant}\).
  • Quadratic Functions: The average rate of change is itself a linear function of the input. Consecutive equal-interval differences of AROC are constant (constant second differences).
  • Vertex & Symmetry: A quadratic function \(f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c\) changes direction at its vertex \(x = -\dfrac{b}{2a}\), where the instantaneous rate of change transitions from positive to negative (or vice versa).

docs.title: 📐 Essential Formulas & Definitions
docs.text:
Linear Constant Rate of Change:

\[f(x) = mx + b \implies \text{AROC}_{[x_1, x_2]} = m \quad \text{for all } x_1 \neq x_2\]

Quadratic Vertex Location:

\[f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c \implies x_{\text{vertex}} = -\frac{b}{2a}\]

AP Exam Tip

To verify if tabular data represents a quadratic function over equally spaced inputs, check if the first differences are changing linearly (i.e., the second differences are constant).

• Fundamental Theorem of Algebra: A polynomial of degree \(n \ge 1\) has exactly \(n\) complex zeros, counted with multiplicity.
  • Complex Conjugate Root Theorem: If a polynomial with real coefficients has a non-real complex zero \(a + bi\), then its conjugate \(a - bi\) is also a zero.
  • Multiplicity Behavior on Graphs:
    • Odd Multiplicity (\(m = 1, 3, \dots\)): The graph crosses the \(x\)-axis at the root.
    • Even Multiplicity (\(m = 2, 4, \dots\)): The graph touches (bounces off) the \(x\)-axis.

docs.title: 📐 Essential Formulas & Definitions
docs.text:
Linear Factorization Theorem:

\[P(x) = a_n (x - z_1)(x - z_2)\cdots(x - z_n) \quad (z_i \in \mathbb{C})\]

AP Exam Tip

Non-real complex zeros always appear in conjugate pairs \((a \pm bi)\) for polynomials with real coefficients. If degree \(n\) is odd, the polynomial must have at least one real zero!

• Leading Term Dominance: As \(x \to \pm\infty\), the highest degree term \(a_n x^n\) dominates all lower-degree terms.
  • Limit Notation: End behavior must be articulated using formal calculus limits: \(\lim_{x \to \infty} P(x)\) and \(\lim_{x \to -\infty} P(x)\).
  • Even vs. Odd Degree Rules:
    • Even Degree (\(n\) even, \(a_n > 0\)): Both ends point up: \(\lim_{x \to \pm\infty} P(x) = \infty\).
    • Even Degree (\(n\) even, \(a_n < 0\)): Both ends point down: \(\lim_{x \to \pm\infty} P(x) = -\infty\).
    • Odd Degree (\(n\) odd, \(a_n > 0\)): Left end down, right end up: \(\lim_{x \to -\infty} P(x) = -\infty\), \(\lim_{x \to \infty} P(x) = \infty\).
    • Odd Degree (\(n\) odd, \(a_n < 0\)): Left end up, right end down: \(\lim_{x \to -\infty} P(x) = \infty\), \(\lim_{x \to \infty} P(x) = -\infty\).

docs.title: 📐 Essential Formulas & Definitions
docs.text:
Polynomial End Behavior Dominance:

\[\lim_{x \to \pm\infty} P(x) = \lim_{x \to \pm\infty} a_n x^n\]

AP Exam Tip

Never write arrow notation like "\(x \to \infty, y \to \infty\)" on the AP Exam unless explicitly instructed. Always write formal limit notation: \(\lim_{x \to \infty} f(x) = \infty\).

• Horizontal Asymptotes: Governed by comparing numerator degree \(n\) and denominator degree \(m\) of \(R(x) = \dfrac{P(x)}{Q(x)}\):
    • \(n < m\): Horizontal asymptote at \(y = 0\).
    • \(n = m\): Horizontal asymptote at \(y = \dfrac{a_n}{b_m}\) (ratio of leading coefficients).
    • \(n > m\): No horizontal asymptote.
  • Slant (Oblique) Asymptotes: Occur when numerator degree is exactly one higher than denominator degree (\(n = m + 1\)). Found via polynomial division: \(R(x) = (mx + b) + \dfrac{r(x)}{Q(x)}\).

docs.title: 📐 Essential Formulas & Definitions
docs.text:
Horizontal Asymptote Limit Definition:

\[\lim_{x \to \infty} R(x) = L \quad \text{or} \quad \lim_{x \to -\infty} R(x) = L \implies y = L \text{ is a horizontal asymptote}\]

AP Exam Tip

A rational function can intersect its horizontal asymptote for small values of \(x\). Horizontal asymptotes describe only global end behavior as \(x \to \pm\infty\), unlike vertical asymptotes which can never be crossed.

  • Sign Charts: Partitioning the domain using all real zeros and vertical asymptotes as boundary test points to establish intervals where \(R(x) > 0\) and \(R(x) < 0\).

Always check candidate zeros in the denominator before declaring them as \(x\)-intercepts! If a candidate makes both numerator and denominator zero, it is a hole, not a real zero.

• Vertical Asymptotes: Occur at \(x = c\) where the denominator equals zero after all common factors with the numerator have been canceled.
  • One-Sided Limit Characterization: The function approaches \(\infty\) or \(-\infty\) from each side:
  • \[\lim_{x \to c^+} R(x) = \pm\infty \quad \text{and} \quad \lim_{x \to c^-} R(x) = \pm\infty\]
  • Multiplicity Rule for Asymptotes:
    • Odd Multiplicity in Denominator: The curve goes to opposite infinities on either side of the asymptote.
    • Even Multiplicity in Denominator: The curve goes to the same infinity on both sides of the asymptote.

docs.title: 📐 Essential Formulas & Definitions
docs.text:
Vertical Asymptote Limit Criterion:

\[\lim_{x \to c^+} f(x) = \pm\infty \quad \text{or} \quad \lim_{x \to c^-} f(x) = \pm\infty \implies x = c \text{ is a vertical asymptote}\]

AP Exam Tip

Vertical asymptotes must be written as linear equations \(x = c\). Writing just the number "\(c\)" on an AP exam will result in loss of credit.

• Arithmetic Sequences: Additive constant common difference \(d\). Successive terms change by addition: \(a_n = a_{n-1} + d\). Discrete analog of linear functions.
  • Geometric Sequences: Multiplicative constant common ratio \(r\). Successive terms change by multiplication: \(g_n = g_{n-1} \cdot r\). Discrete analog of exponential functions.

\[g_n = g_1 \cdot r^{n - 1}\]

Notice the \((n - 1)\) exponent in geometric sequences when index starts at \(n = 1\). When index starts at \(n = 0\), the formula simplifies to \(g_n = g_0 \cdot r^n\).

docs.text:
• Linear Change: Over equal input intervals \(\Delta x\), the output changes by a constant difference \(\Delta y = m \Delta x\).
  • Exponential Change: Over equal input intervals \(\Delta x\), the output changes by a constant ratio / factor \(\dfrac{f(x + \Delta x)}{f(x)} = b^{\Delta x}\).
  • Data Identification: Test table outputs: if \(y_{k+1} - y_k = \text{const} \implies\) linear; if \(y_{k+1} / y_k = \text{const} \implies\) exponential.

docs.title: 📐 Essential Formulas & Definitions
docs.text:
Exponential Constant Ratio Property:

\[\frac{f(x + c)}{f(x)} = b^c = \text{constant for any fixed } c\]

AP Exam Tip

If inputs are not spaced by \(1\), compute the base using \(b = \left(\frac{y_2}{y_1}\right)^{1 / (x_2 - x_1)}\).

docs.text:
• Standard Form: \(f(x) = a \cdot b^x\) where \(a \neq 0\), \(b > 0\), and \(b \neq 1\).
  • Growth vs. Decay:
    • \(b > 1\): Exponential Growth (\(f(x)\) increases as \(x\) increases).
    • \(0 < b < 1\): Exponential Decay (\(f(x)\) decreases as \(x\) increases).
  • Key Features:
    • Horizontal Asymptote at \(y = 0\).
    • \(y\)-intercept at \((0, a)\).
    • Domain: \((-\infty, \infty)\); Range: \((0, \infty)\) for \(a > 0\).

docs.title: 📐 Essential Formulas & Definitions
docs.text:
Exponential Function Form:

\[f(x) = a \cdot b^x = a(1 + r)^x\]

AP Exam Tip

The base \(b\) can NEVER be negative! If \(b < 0\), the expression \((-2)^x\) is not defined for fractional exponents in real numbers.

\[a \cdot (b^k)^x = a \cdot (b)^{kx}\]

AP Exam Tip

To find the percent change per unit time from \(f(t) = a \cdot b^{kt}\), rewrite the base as \((b^k)^t\). The effective growth rate per unit time is \(r = b^k - 1\).

• Discrete Compounding: \(A(t) = P\left(1 + \dfrac{r}{n}\right)^{nt}\) where \(P\) is principal, \(r\) is annual rate, \(n\) is compoundings per year.
  • Continuous Compounding & Natural Base \(e\): \(A(t) = P e^{rt}\).

  • Doubling Time: \(P(t) = P_0 (2)^{t / t_d}\).

• Asymptotic Dominance: Exponential growth functions (\(b > 1\)) eventually outgrow any polynomial function of degree \(n\), no matter how large the leading coefficient or degree.
  • Model Evaluation: Examining residuals and domain constraints to determine which function model provides the most valid physical interpretation.

docs.title: 📐 Essential Formulas & Definitions
docs.text:
Asymptotic Dominance Limit:

\[\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{a \cdot b^x}{c \cdot x^n} = \infty \quad (b > 1, \; c > 0)\]

AP Exam Tip

Even though a polynomial like \(y = 1{,}000 x^{10}\) may be much larger than \(y = 1.01^x\) for small values of \(x\), the exponential model will ALWAYS exceed the polynomial for sufficiently large \(x\).

• Definition: \((f \circ g)(x) = f(g(x))\). The output of \(g\) becomes the direct input to \(f\).
  • Domain of Composite Function: All inputs \(x\) in the domain of \(g\) such that \(g(x)\) is within the domain of \(f\):
  • \[\text{Domain}(f \circ g) = \{x \in \text{Domain}(g) \mid g(x) \in \text{Domain}(f)\}\]
  • Decomposition: Breaking a composite expression into distinct inner and outer component functions.

docs.title: 📐 Essential Formulas & Definitions
docs.text:
Function Composition:

\[(f \circ g)(x) = f\big(g(x)\big)\]

AP Exam Tip

To find the domain of \(f(g(x))\), first restrict \(x\) to the domain of inner function \(g\). Then solve the inequality requiring \(g(x)\) to satisfy the domain conditions of outer function \(f\).

docs.text:
• Invertibility Condition: A function has an inverse function if and only if it is one-to-one (passes the Horizontal Line Test).
  • Algebraic Method: Set \(y = f(x)\), swap \(x\) and \(y\), and solve for \(y = f^{-1}(x)\).
  • Graphical Reflection: The graph of \(f^{-1}(x)\) is the reflection of \(f(x)\) across the line \(y = x\). If \((a, b)\) is on \(f\), then \((b, a)\) is on \(f^{-1}\).
  • Inverse Verification: \(f(f^{-1}(x)) = x\) for all \(x\) in domain of \(f^{-1}\), and \(f^{-1}(f(x)) = x\) for all \(x\) in domain of \(f\).

docs.title: 📐 Essential Formulas & Definitions
docs.text:
Inverse Function Composition Identity:

\[f\big(f^{-1}(x)\big) = x \quad \text{and} \quad f^{-1}\big(f(x)\big) = x\]

AP Exam Tip

The symbol \(f^{-1}(x)\) means the inverse function, NOT the reciprocal \(\frac{1}{f(x)}\)! The reciprocal is denoted as \([f(x)]^{-1}\).
